title: [Vantage Point] GMA’s cash cushion shrinks as the boob tube goes digital
summary: Today, competing against global streaming giants and social media algorithms has changed the math entirely

blocks.text: As the Philippines prepares to switch off analog television signals in Mega Manila, the country’s biggest television groups are facing a severe financial reckoning. Industry leader GMA Network saw its profit for the first nine months plunge, while rival ABS-CBN reported a consolidated net loss over the same period.

For decades, the Filipino living room revolved around a single glowing box. Families gathered around television sets with rabbit-ear antennas to watch noontime variety shows, tearjerking dramas, and nightly newscasts.
That familiar era is officially winding down.

Starting in January 2027, the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) is scheduled to pull the plug on traditional analog television broadcasts, beginning in Mega Manila—covering Metro Manila, Bulacan, Cavite, Pampanga, Bataan, Laguna, and Rizal—where most households have already shifted to digital signals.

Viewers whose television sets lack a compatible digital tuner will need to buy a digital set-top box, which typically costs between P500 and P800, just to keep their old sets working. Compatible digital televisions can receive the signals directly with a suitable antenna. Cable and satellite subscribers will not be affected by the terrestrial analog switch-off.

While the technical move is a routine upgrade in broadcast engineering, it arrives at a painful moment for the country’s free-to-air television networks. Behind the scenes, the business model that built Philippine broadcast empires is rapidly unraveling.
Take GMA Network, the undisputed king of Philippine television after its longtime rival ABS-CBN lost its broadcast franchise in 2020.

On paper, GMA remains dominant. According to Nielsen ratings, it stayed as the number-one station nationwide through the first nine months of 2026, powered by flagship programs like 24 Oras and Kapuso Mo, Jessica Soho, alongside top-performing radio stations Super Radyo DZBB and Barangay LS 97.1.
Yet GMA’s latest financial report, released on November 13, reads less like a victory lap and more like a warning siren.

blocks.caption: Industry disruption continues: GMA’s profit falls 98% in Q3, ABS-CBN still in red

blocks.text: To understand how sharply GMA’s fortunes turned in the first nine months of 2026, imagine a neighborhood store that usually records P100 in daily profit after deducting its expenses and taxes. Suddenly, that profit shrinks to less than P2.

That is essentially what happened to GMA. Its consolidated net income—the profit left over after deducting all expenses and taxes—plunged by 98%, tumbling from P2.07 billion in January–September 2025 to P32.85 million in the same period this year. The third quarter alone produced a P77.37-million loss, reversing a P102-million profit a year earlier.

Why did profits evaporate so fast? Look at the money coming through the door. Total revenues for the first nine months dropped 31%, wiping out P4.32 billion in sales. Because free-to-air television relies heavily on commercials to pay the bills, advertising is the lifeblood of the business. During January–September, GMA’s advertising revenue fell by a third, sliding from P12.82 billion last year to P8.64 billion.

Part of this drop comes down to the calendar. The first nine months of 2025 benefited from political advertisements tied to the May midterm elections, a temporary windfall that vanished in 2026. But GMA also acknowledged softer recurring revenues, showing that the deterioration extended beyond the election cycle.

Even setting election spending aside, regular corporate advertisers are tightening their belts. GMA pointed to everyday operational headaches—high fuel prices, stubborn inflation, rising utility and labor costs, and supply chain snags linked to conflict in the Middle East—that squeezed advertisers’ margins and prompted them to reduce spending. GMA itself cut total operating expenses by 13%, but those savings could not keep pace with the 31% revenue decline.

GMA’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA), fell 68%, dropping from P4.56 billion to P1.47 billion in the first nine months. EBITDA measures earnings before those charges; it is not operating cash flow. Actual operating cash flow fell from P4.34 billion to P1.63 billion.

Simply put, the network’s cash generation has weakened dramatically. Notably, GMA revealed that digital ads remain its second-biggest revenue contributor, although that ranking alone does not establish how quickly audiences or advertising budgets are migrating online.
The reckoning spreads across the dial.
If the industry leader is struggling to stay in the black, the picture is even bleaker elsewhere on the dial. (READ: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way)

ABS-CBN Corporation, still led by the Lopez family six years after losing its broadcast franchise, remains deep in the red. For the first nine months of 2026, the company posted a consolidated net loss of P2.96 billion, widening by 32% from P2.24 billion a year earlier. Its third-quarter loss, however, narrowed to P1.13 billion from P1.39 billion. These are accounting losses, rather than a direct measure of cash spending exceeding cash receipts.

blocks.caption: ABS-CBN is now 84% content — and still losing money. Can P6 billion fix it?

blocks.text: Total revenues at ABS-CBN slipped 11% in the first nine months, moving from P11.75 billion in 2025 to P10.52 billion. Third-quarter revenue nevertheless increased to P3.63 billion from P3.48 billion.

Without its old nationwide broadcast franchise, ABS-CBN has reinvented itself as a content studio and digital player. It now produces shows for former rivals GMA and TV5, sells programs overseas, and leans heavily on live entertainment. (READ: Streaming services ‘winning hearts and minds’ of Filipinos, says new study)

The May 2026 Star Cinema movie Tayo Sa Wakas, starring Donny Pangilinan and Belle Mariano, alongside girl group BINI’s Coachella appearance and global tour, contributed to ABS-CBN’s activities during the period. These ventures broaden its revenue sources, although their contribution must ultimately be judged against production, talent, promotion, and distribution costs.
All three major free-to-air networks now face financial difficulties, and the Philippine advertising pie is simply too small to sustain fierce, three-way competition.
For decades, regulators and viewers assumed that more networks meant healthier competition. Today, competing against global streaming giants and social media algorithms has changed the math entirely.

As analog signals fade to black in Mega Manila in January, Philippine television faces a sobering truth. Although buying a P500 converter box can rescue an old television set from the junkyard, saving the networks that fill those screens will require a far deeper reinvention. – Rappler.com
